NFL Overtime Betting: How the Guaranteed-Possession Rule Changed the Numbers

Published September 18, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

For most of the sport's history, an NFL overtime coin toss was one of the more quietly decisive moments a bettor could watch unfold. Win the flip, elect to receive, and a team had a real shot at ending the game without its defense ever taking the field. That changed for the postseason in 2022 and, as of the 2025 season, for the regular season too: every team now gets a possession in overtime unless the first team to have the ball scores a touchdown. It's a small-sounding tweak to a niche situation, but it forced sportsbooks to rebuild how they price the minutes after regulation, and it's worth understanding if you bet live or shop overtime markets at all.

The rule, then and now

Before 2010, NFL overtime was pure sudden death: first score of any kind ended the game. From 2010 through 2021, the league softened that slightly — if the team that won the toss and received the ball scored only a field goal on its opening drive, the opponent got a chance to answer. A touchdown on that first drive, though, still ended things instantly, no matter how the rest of the roster felt about it.

Owners changed the postseason version of the rule in March 2022, guaranteeing both teams at least one possession in playoff overtime regardless of how the first drive ended — the only exception being a defensive score. That left a strange split for three seasons: fairer rules in January, old rules the rest of the year. At the March 2025 league meeting, owners voted to extend the guaranteed-possession format to the regular season as well, closing that gap. Every NFL overtime period played since has followed the same structure: both teams get the ball unless the first offense punches in a touchdown, and if the score is still tied after one ten-minute overtime period in the regular season, the game ends in a tie rather than continuing into a second period.

Why the old coin toss moved live odds so much

The scale of the old advantage is easy to understate until you see the numbers. Across NFL history under the pre-2010 and 2010-2021 sudden-death formats, teams that won the coin toss and elected to receive won regular-season overtime games at roughly a 58% clip — a record in the neighborhood of 54 wins to 39 losses with a handful of ties, well outside what a 50/50 coin flip should produce on its own. The gap was even more extreme in the smaller postseason sample: from 2010 through 2021, teams that won the toss and received went 10-2 in the games that reached overtime under that modified format, with seven of those games ending on an opening-drive touchdown before the other offense ever touched the ball.

Sportsbooks priced around that reality. A live moneyline posted the instant overtime began — before either team had run a snap — had to bake in a meaningful, verifiable edge for whichever team had just won the toss, not a coin-flip 50/50 split. That's the specific distortion the rule change was designed to remove, and it's also the specific line-pricing habit bettors who grew up on the old rule sometimes carry into today's games without realizing the underlying math changed.

Why it mattered to bettors: under the old rule, the biggest single edge in an NFL overtime period often belonged to whoever won a coin flip, not whoever had the better roster on the field. That's no longer true in the same way.

How live win-probability models had to be rebuilt

Live betting models lean heavily on win-probability curves that update after every play, and the coin-toss result used to be a major early input in overtime specifically. Under sudden death, a model had good reason to shift several points toward the receiving team the moment the toss was announced, because history showed that team closing out the game outright a clear majority of the time. Under the guaranteed-possession rule, that same coin toss carries far less standalone weight — the receiving team still gets the first crack at the end zone and the choice of whether to play for six or hedge for three, but a made field goal no longer ends the discussion, and a defensive stop no longer eliminates a team's chance to answer.

In practice, that means live win-probability swings around the coin toss itself are smaller and more conservative than they were a few seasons ago, and the bigger swings now come later — after the first drive's actual result is known, whether that's a touchdown (game over), a field goal or punt (opponent gets its own possession, often with clearer information about what number it needs to beat), or a turnover.

A worked example: pricing the coin toss then vs. now

Picture a tied game heading to overtime between two closely matched teams, each a true 50/50 shot in regulation. Under the pre-2022/pre-2025 sudden-death rule, a book posting a live line the instant the receiving team was decided might have shown that team around -140 to -150 on the moneyline (implying roughly a 58-60% win probability) purely off historical coin-toss outcomes, before a single snap. Under today's guaranteed-possession format, that same moment produces a far tamer number — something closer to -110 to -120 for the receiving team, reflecting a modest first-possession edge (they control tempo and get the first look at the end zone) rather than a near-decisive one. The receiving team is still slightly favored to win overtime, just nowhere near as heavily, because a field goal or a stop no longer settles anything by itself.

That gap matters directly to anyone betting the live overtime line in the seconds after the toss: the "obvious" advantage bettors remember from a decade of sudden-death overtime is now worth roughly a third of what it used to be in moneyline terms.

Overtime totals, props, and the "double OT" tail

The guaranteed-possession rule also reshaped overtime totals and prop markets, not just the moneyline. Because the trailing team on the first drive now always gets a real answer opportunity, overtime periods run slightly longer on average than they did under pure sudden death, which nudges overtime-period point totals up modestly and gives "will the game go to a second overtime" props more room to hit in the postseason, where play continues until a winner is decided. In the regular season, the ten-minute period cap and the tie-if-still-level rule cut the other way — bettors betting an overtime total need to remember regular-season overtime can simply end in a tie if nobody scores again after the opening exchange, which caps how high some totals markets can reasonably run compared to playoff overtime, where the game keeps going.

Player prop markets built around "next score" or "overtime touchdown scorer" also shifted: with the opposing offense guaranteed a real look regardless of how the first drive ends, oddsmakers can no longer treat the receiving team's opening possession as the de facto end of the scoring opportunities for the prop's settlement window.

Old rule vs. new rule, side by side

FeatureSudden death (pre-2022 postseason / pre-2025 regular season)Guaranteed possession (current, leaguewide)
Opening-drive touchdownGame over instantlyGame over instantly (unchanged)
Opening-drive field goalOpponent gets a possession (2010-2021 only; true sudden death before that)Opponent gets a possession
Opening-drive punt/turnoverGame could end on the very next defensive or special-teams scoreOpponent still guaranteed a possession first
Regular-season deadlockContinues until a score (older eras) or ends in a tie after one periodEnds in a tie after one ten-minute period if still level
Receiving team's historical win rate~58% (regular season, sudden-death era)Meaningfully closer to 50/50

Mistakes bettors still make with the new format

The most common error is simple inertia: treating the coin toss the way bettors did five or six seasons ago and assuming the receiving team carries a near-decisive edge live. A second mistake is ignoring the regular-season tie rule entirely when shopping overtime totals or "will there be a winner" markets — a tie is a real, priced-in outcome in the regular season that doesn't exist in the postseason, and conflating the two formats leads to misreading a number that looks "off" but isn't. A third is underestimating how much the opening drive's actual result — not just who has the ball — now drives the live line; a stalled three-and-out on the first possession moves a model's numbers far more than the toss itself does under the current rule.

If you're newer to live NFL betting generally, our guide on how second-half and quarter lines are priced covers the broader mechanics of in-game repricing that also apply once a game reaches overtime.

Frequently asked questions

Does the guaranteed-possession rule apply to every NFL game now?

Yes. It applied only to the postseason starting in 2022, but NFL owners voted in March 2025 to extend the same format to regular-season games as well, so every overtime period across the full season now follows it.

Can a regular-season NFL game still end in a tie?

Yes. If the score is still level after one ten-minute overtime period in the regular season, the game ends in a tie. Playoff games are different — they continue with additional overtime periods until a winner is determined.

Is the coin toss still worth anything for the receiving team?

Somewhat, but far less than under the old sudden-death rule. The receiving team still gets the first possession and controls tempo and play-calling first, which is a real but modest edge — not the near-decisive advantage a coin flip used to hand out when a made field goal could end the game outright.

Why did the old rule get changed in the first place?

Widely cited numbers from the sudden-death era — including a run of playoff games where the receiving team scored a touchdown on its opening possession and won without the opponent's offense taking a single snap — pushed the league toward a format seen as fairer to both teams.
